points: 〜なければいけません / 〜なきゃいけません

title: Obligation · probably
titleJp: 行かなければいけません
canDo: I can say what I have to do with 〜なければいけません, in the present and in the past (〜なければいけませんでした).
I can build なければ from the ない-form of any verb, including する, 来る and verbs ending in う (使わなければ).
I can recognize the casual forms 〜なきゃ and 〜なくちゃ and use them with friends.
I can say that something will probably happen with (たぶん) 〜でしょう, and ask a more polite question with 〜でしょうか.
I can use でしょう↗, with a rising voice, to check that the listener agrees ("…, right?").

blocks.t: Session 1 · Warm-up: say the ない-form of 起きる, 働く, 使う, 飲む, 帰る, 待つ, する and 来る out loud
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each word and repeat it twice
Grammar 4a (〜なければいけません) and 4b (〜でしょう): the examples aloud + one 🔬 for each
Block 6: the Lesson 12 video or the Sakubi sections, as a second explanation (read to understand, not to memorize)
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Session 2 (it can be on another day): Workbook pp. 117–118 (the lesson's review and listening) and the Lesson 12 kanji on pp. 151–152
Checklist (block 10) + write your questions in the lesson notebook

skills: The ない-form of every verb, without hesitating (lesson 08-1). なければ comes straight from it.
〜ては いけません, "you must not" (lesson 06-3). You will need to tell "must not" apart from "have to".
〜と 思います for giving an opinion (lesson 08-2), to compare it with でしょう.
〜ので, 〜んです and 〜ほうが いいです (lessons 12-1 and 12-2), which appear in the examples and the homework.
The Lesson 12 kanji (早, 起, 使, 働, 度…) appear in the sentences, always with the kana next to them.

vocab.en: to wake up, to get up
to call, to phone (〜に 電話する = to call someone)
to hand in (an assignment); to take out
to take (a train, a bus), to get on (電車に のる)

grammar.title: 〜なければいけません / 〜なきゃ
grammar.explanation:
To say you **have to** do something, Japanese uses a double negative: "**if** I **don't** do it, **it's no good**". なければ = "if (I) don't…"; いけません = "it won't do, it's not OK", the same いけません as in 〜ては いけません (lesson 06-3). Put together: have to. English says "must" directly; Japanese gets there through two negatives.
• Formation: take the **ない-form** and change the final い to **ければ**. 行かない → 行かなければ; 食べない → 食べなければ; しない → しなければ; 来ない → 来なければ (こなければ). Then add いけません or なりません. This ければ is the **"if" form** (the ば-form): ない conjugates like an い-adjective, and い-words make "if" with ければ. You will study that form on its own in lesson 22-2.
• Verbs ending in う make their ない-form with わ: 使う → 使わない → 使わなければいけません.
• **いけません × なりません**: the meaning is practically the same. なりません sounds a little more formal and shows up more in **rules** and written texts; in conversation, いけません is more common.
• **Past** ("I had to"): only the end changes. 行かなければいけませんでした.
• **Casual**: 〜なければいけない / 〜なければならない. In everyday speech you get the contractions **〜なきゃ** (なければ → なけりゃ → なきゃ) and **〜なくちゃ** (from 〜なくては, another form with the same meaning): 行かなきゃ いけない, 行かなくちゃ. Often the rest drops off and the sentence ends right there: 行かなきゃ。 ("I've got to go!"). Among friends, the "no good" part can also be だめ: 行かなきゃ だめだよ。 Use all of these with friends, not with your teacher.
• In the sentence, 起きなければいけません is **a single block**, and it is the predicate. ヅオリンゴー's Anatomy reads that block as a **PREDICATE (obligation)**. Find it at the end and read it first: I have to → what? → get up → when? → at six.
• **Going further (Sakubi):** there are several more versions of the same double negative — 〜なくては いけない (the full form behind なくちゃ), and, in formal writing, 〜ねば ならない. They differ a little in flavor and strength, but even for native speakers the difference is subtle: recognize them all as "must", and use なければいけません yourself.
grammar.structure: [ない-form without the い] + ければ いけません / なりません · casual: 〜なきゃ / 〜なくちゃ

examples.jp: 毎朝 六時に 起きなければいけません。
examples.kana: まいあさ ろくじに おきなければいけません。
examples.en: I have to get up at six every morning. [lit. every morning, if I don't get up at six, it won't do]

examples.jp: レポートは 日本語で 書かなければなりません。
examples.kana: レポートは にほんごで かかなければなりません。
examples.romaji: Repōto wa nihongo de kakanakereba narimasen.
examples.en: The report has to be written in Japanese.

examples.jp: あ、もう 十時だ。母に 電話しなきゃ。
examples.kana: あ、もう じゅうじだ。ははに でんわしなきゃ。
examples.romaji: A, mō jūji da. Haha ni denwa shinakya.
examples.en: Oh, it's already ten. I've got to call my mom! (casual)

pitfalls: Don't confuse it with the prohibition from lesson 06-3: 行っては いけません = "you must not go"; 行かなければいけません = "you have to go".
The base is the ない-form, not the ます stem — and verbs ending in う use わ: 行きなければ ✗ → 行かなければ ✓; 使あなければ ✗ → 使わなければ ✓.
なきゃ and なくちゃ are spoken, casual forms. In a message to your teacher or boss: 休まなきゃ いけません ✗ → 休まなければいけません ✓.
As in English, "don't have to" is not "must not", and it is not the negative of this form either. "You don't have to do it" is 〜なくても いいです, which you will see in lesson 17-2.
howToStudy: Tap 🔬 on example 1: Anatomy reads 起きなければいけません as one PREDICATE block (obligation), and both 毎朝 and 六時に show up as TIME. Read it backwards: I have to get up → at what time? → at six → how often? → every morning.
Conjugation out loud: 8 verbs (起きる, 働く, 使う, 飲む, 帰る, 待つ, する, 来る) → ない-form → なければいけません. Then repeat them all in the casual version with なきゃ.
In your notebook, list 5 real obligations from your routine with 〜なければいけません and 2 that you have already carried out with 〜なければいけませんでした.

grammar.title: 〜でしょう
grammar.explanation:
でしょう expresses **probability**: "probably", "I guess". It is the polite form of だろう. It often comes with **たぶん** before it, adding to the doubt: たぶん 雨でしょう。
• **Where it comes from:** でしょう is です with the same ending as the volitional 行こう ("let's go", lesson 15-1). With a verb, that ending shows intention; with です, it **offers an idea** instead of stating it: not "it is", but "it would be…" → "probably". That is also why でしょう can invite the listener to agree (see ↗ below).
• Formation: **short form + でしょう**. 来る → 来るでしょう; 来ない → 来ないでしょう; さむい → さむいでしょう; 帰った → 帰ったでしょう.
• With **nouns and な-adjectives** in the present affirmative, だ **disappears**, and な does not come in either: 雨でしょう, しずかでしょう. Notice the difference: 〜んです and 〜ので swap だ for な; でしょう just drops だ.
• It is the typical language of the **weather forecast**. In conversation, to give your own opinion, 〜と 思います (lesson 08-2) is usually more common; でしょう on its own sounds a bit formal.
• **〜でしょうか** is a **more polite, softer** question than 〜ですか. Use it to ask carefully, to a stranger or someone above you, or to ask for someone's opinion.
• **でしょう↗**, with the voice rising at the end, asks for **confirmation**: "…, right?", when you think the other person knows or agrees. おいしいでしょう↗ = "it's good, right?". It can sound like a reproach: きのう 言ったでしょう↗ = "I told you yesterday, didn't I?". In casual speech it becomes でしょ↗ or だろう↗.
• In the sentence, でしょう sits at the **end of the predicate** and changes the tone of the whole sentence: the statement becomes a guess.
grammar.structure: [short form] でしょう · [N / な-adj] でしょう (no だ) · 〜でしょうか (polite question)

examples.jp: あしたの リオは 雨でしょう。
examples.kana: あしたの リオは あめでしょう。
examples.romaji: Ashita no Rio wa ame deshō.
examples.en: Tomorrow it will probably rain in Rio. [lit. as for tomorrow's Rio, it is probably rain]

examples.jp: ルーカスさんは かぜなので、たぶん 来ないでしょう。
examples.kana: ルーカスさんは かぜなので、たぶん こないでしょう。
examples.romaji: Rūkasu-san wa kaze na node, tabun konai deshō.
examples.en: Lucas has a cold, so he probably won't come.

examples.jp: 先生、今 ちょっと いいでしょうか。
examples.kana: せんせい、いま ちょっと いいでしょうか。
examples.romaji: Sensei, ima chotto ii deshō ka.
examples.en: Sensei, would you have a moment now? [lit. teacher, now, a little, would it be OK?]

pitfalls: With nouns and な-adjectives, no だ and no な: 雨だでしょう ✗, 雨なでしょう ✗ → 雨でしょう ✓.
でしょう is not for your own plans, because you know those: あした 行くでしょう。 ✗ → あした 行きます。 ✓.
でしょう↘ ("probably") and でしょう↗ ("…, right?") are written the same way: the difference is the intonation. In writing, the context (and sometimes a ？) shows which one it is.
With a teacher or a boss, don't use でしょう↗ to check, because it can sound like a reproach. Use 〜ですよね。 instead.
howToStudy: Be the weather presenter: say out loud the forecast for 4 cities (サンパウロ, リオ, 東京, きょうと) with でしょう: 雨でしょう, さむいでしょう, 雪でしょう, くもりでしょう.
Tap 🔬 on example 2 and name the blocks: かぜなので shows up as REASON, たぶん as HOW / HOW OFTEN, and 来ないでしょう is the PREDICATE, with でしょう at the end turning the statement into a guess.
Speaking with intonation: record 3 sentences with でしょう↘ (probably) and the same 3 with でしょう↗ (…, right?). Listen and check that the difference is audible.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook. Write the Japanese with the kanji you already know and kana for the rest. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day.

tasks.prompt: Turn each sentence into an obligation with 〜なければいけません. Follow the instruction in brackets when there is one.

items.q: くすりを 飲みます。

a.jp: くすりを 飲まなければいけません。
a.kana: くすりを のまなければいけません。

items.q: 日本語を 使います。

a.jp: 日本語を 使わなければいけません。
a.kana: にほんごを つかわなければいけません。

items.note: 使う → 使わない: verbs ending in う make their ない-form with わ.

items.q: あした 病院に 来ます。

a.jp: あした 病院に 来なければいけません。
a.kana: あした びょういんに こなければいけません。

items.note: 来る → 来ない (こない) → 来なければ (こなければ).

items.q: しゅくだいを します。

a.jp: しゅくだいを しなければいけません。

items.q: きのう 早く 起きました。(past: "had to")

a.jp: きのう 早く 起きなければいけませんでした。
a.kana: きのう はやく おきなければいけませんでした。

items.note: In the past, only the end changes: いけませんでした.

items.q: 電車に のります。(casual, with なきゃ)

a.jp: 電車に のらなきゃ。
a.kana: でんしゃに のらなきゃ。

items.note: のる is an う-verb (のらない). なくちゃ also works: 電車に のらなくちゃ。

tasks.prompt: Fill in でしょう (or でしょうか) in the right form. Watch out for nouns and な-adjectives.

items.q: その 町は ＿＿＿＿。(しずか · probably)
items.note: A な-adjective: no な and no だ.

items.q: 田中さんは もう ＿＿＿＿。(帰った · probably)
items.note: "Mr. Tanaka has probably gone home already."

items.q: すみません、えきは ＿＿＿＿。(どこ · polite question)
items.note: でしょうか sounds softer than どこですか.

items.q: この ケーキ、＿＿＿＿↗ (おいしい · asking a friend to agree)
items.note: The voice rises at the end: "it's good, right?". Among close friends, also でしょ？

tasks.prompt: Translate into Japanese. Some items review lessons 12-1 and 12-2.

items.q: I have to go to the hospital tomorrow.

a.jp: あした 病院に 行かなければいけません。
a.kana: あした びょういんに いかなければいけません。

items.q: I have a fever of 38 degrees, so I have to take today off work.

a.jp: ねつが 三十八度 あるので、きょうは 仕事を 休まなければいけません。
a.kana: ねつが さんじゅうはちど あるので、きょうは しごとを やすまなければいけません。
a.romaji: Netsu ga sanjūhachido aru node, kyō wa shigoto o yasumanakereba ikemasen.

items.q: Maria probably knows. — Right, we'd better ask her.

a.jp: マリアさんは たぶん 知っているでしょう。— ええ、マリアさんに 聞いた ほうが いいですね。
a.kana: マリアさんは たぶん しっているでしょう。— ええ、マリアさんに きいた ほうが いいですね。
a.romaji: Maria-san wa tabun shitte iru deshō. — Ee, Maria-san ni kiita hō ga ii desu ne.

items.q: Sensei, is this answer OK? (as politely as you can)

a.jp: 先生、この こたえで いいでしょうか。
a.kana: せんせい、この こたえで いいでしょうか。
a.romaji: Sensei, kono kotae de ii deshō ka.

items.note: 〜で いいですか = "is it OK like this?". With でしょうか, the question becomes more careful.

tasks.prompt: You woke up with a fever and can't go to work (or to college). In 4–5 sentences, write the 連絡 message (see Culture) to your boss or teacher: explain with 〜ので or 〜んです, say what you have to do with 〜なければいけません and end with a polite request in 〜でしょうか. Then read it aloud as if it were a phone call.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: おはようございます。ルーカスです。すみません、ねつが 三十八度 あるので、きょうは 休みます。午後 病院に 行かなければいけません。レポートは あした 出しても いいでしょうか。
a.kana: おはようございます。ルーカスです。すみません、ねつが さんじゅうはちど あるので、きょうは やすみます。ごご びょういんに いかなければいけません。レポートは あした だしても いいでしょうか。
a.romaji: Ohayō gozaimasu. Rūkasu desu. Sumimasen, netsu ga sanjūhachido aru node, kyō wa yasumimasu. Gogo byōin ni ikanakereba ikemasen. Repōto wa ashita dashite mo ii deshō ka.
a.en: Good morning. This is Lucas. I'm sorry, I have a fever of 38 degrees, so I'm taking today off. I have to go to the doctor in the afternoon. Would it be all right if I handed in the report tomorrow?

items.note: Check: the reason with ので (or んです) comes before the result; なければ comes from the ない-form (行かない → 行かなければ); and the request ends in でしょうか, which sounds softer than ですか.

workbook.tip: A review of all of Lesson 12: do it in session 2, after lessons 12-1 to 12-3.
You need the Workbook audio. Do it in session 2 and check it with the official Genki Answer Key.
The Lesson 12 kanji. First practice the stroke order in Kanji → ✍️ Write, in ヅオリンゴー.
Do it after page 151 and check it with the official Genki Answer Key.

practice.what: Play normally and hunt the dialogues for obligations and guesses: 〜なければ, 〜なきゃ, 〜なくちゃ, 〜でしょう, 〜だろう. When you find one, pause and say out loud whether it means "have to" or "probably". Log the session in Immersion → Games and paste one of those lines into 🔬 Anatomy. Save the clearest one in Mining, with every word looked up.

Lesson 12 vocabulary in the SRS (the 🌊 All deck gathers the day's reviews) and Practice L12, now with the whole lesson. Then Drills → 🔬 Anatomy → 🧱 Build from the end: 5 sentences, starting from the obligation block or from でしょう.

Kanji through vocabulary: in Kanji → ✍️ Write, practice the Lesson 12 kanji (昔, 神, 早, 起, 牛, 使, 働, 連, 別, 度, 赤, 青, 色) before Workbook pages 151–152, each inside a word: 昔 (むかし), 神社 (じんじゃ), 早い (はやい), 起きる (おきる), 牛にく (ぎゅうにく), 使う (つかう), 働く (はたらく), 連絡 (れんらく), 〜度 (〜ど), 赤い (あかい), 青い (あおい), 色 (いろ). If kanji keep slipping away, try a short story or picture for each one's parts.

You now have all of Genki I's grammar. You won't remember every point yet — that is normal: reading is what makes grammar stick. In the Resources tab, open Tadoku's free graded readers and read two level-1 or level-2 stories, one per session, for fun. Hunt for 〜なければ and でしょう, and save 1 sentence you like in Mining (look words up with Jisho.org, or with the Yomitan pop-up dictionary on a computer).

Tap 🔊 on each example in this lesson and repeat along 3 times. Compare the でしょう examples: in 雨でしょう the voice falls at the end (it is just a guess); in いいでしょうか it rises slightly on か (it is a question); say おいしいでしょう↗ with a rising voice, to feel the "…, right?". Then record the 連絡 message (homework h4) as if it were a voice message to your boss, in 30 seconds or less.

culture.title: ほうれんそう at work
culture.titleJp: ほうれんそう（報告・連絡・相談）
culture.body: In Japanese companies, almost every new employee hears about **ほうれんそう**. The word means "spinach", but here it is a pun on three habits: **報告** (ほうこく, reporting to your boss on how the work is going), **連絡** (れんらく, letting the people concerned know about a fact, such as a delay or a change of schedule) and **相談** (そうだん, consulting someone before deciding when you are unsure). The idea is for information to flow **early**, bad news included, so that nobody is caught by surprise. So if your train is late or you wake up with a fever, you are expected to let people know right away, usually by phone or message, before your start time. Some people criticize too much ほうれんそう as micromanagement, but the term is still widely used in company training.
culture.try: After writing the homework message (h4), read it aloud, starting with おはようございます。(your name)です。 Then say which of the three (報告, 連絡 or 相談) each sentence of your message stands for.

checklist: I turn any verb into 〜なければいけません (including 使う → 使わなければ, する and 来る), without looking.
I say "I had to" with 〜なければいけませんでした.
I recognize 〜なきゃ and 〜なくちゃ (and 〜なきゃ だめ) in casual speech and know not to use them with my teacher.
I don't confuse 〜なければいけません (have to) with 〜ては いけません (must not).
I make guesses with (たぶん) 〜でしょう, dropping だ after nouns and な-adjectives (雨でしょう, しずかでしょう).
I ask polite questions with 〜でしょうか and use でしょう↗ to check that the listener agrees.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
I did Workbook pages 115–118 and the kanji pages, 151–152.
